metadata.title: Simultaneous determination of two coefficients in the Riemannian hyperbolic equation from boundary measurements

nodes.name: Initial boundary value problem for the wave equation with potential $q$ and absorption coefficient $a$
nodes.statement: We consider the following initial boundary value problem for the wave equation with a potential $q$ and an absorption coefficient $a$, \begin{equation} \left\{ \begin{array}{llll} \para{\partial^2_t-\Op}u=0 & \textrm{in }\; Q,\cr u(\cdot,0 )=\p_tu(\cdot,0)=0 & \textrm{in }\; \M ,\cr u=f & \textrm{on } \; \Sigma. \end{array} \right. \end{equation} Here $a,q:\M\to\R$ are real valued functions in $L^\infty(\M)$ and $f\in H^1(\Sigma)$.
nodes.statement_short: Forward problem: wave equation with damping $a(x)\p_t$ and potential $q(x)$, zero initial data, Dirichlet data $f$ on $\Sigma$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction and main results

nodes.name: Riemannian inner product and norm on the tangent space $T_x\M$
nodes.statement: If we fix local coordinates $x=(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$ and let $\para{\frac{\p\, }{\p x^1},\dots,\frac{\p\,}{\p x^n}}$ denote the corresponding tangent vector fields, the inner product and the norm on the tangent space $T_x\M$ are given by $$ \g(X,Y)=\seq{X,Y}=\sum_{j,k=1}^n\g_{jk}X^jY^k, $$ $$ \abs{X}=\seq{X,X}^{1/2},\qquad X=\sum_{i=1}^nX^i\frac{\p}{\p x^i},\quad Y=\sum_{i=1}^n Y^i\frac{\p}{\p x^i}.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction and main results

nodes.name: Initial boundary value problem with source term $F$
nodes.statement: With these definitions in minds, we consider the following initial boundary value problem for the wave equation \begin{equation} \left\{ \begin{array}{llll} \para{\partial_t^2-\Delta+a(x)\p_t+q(x)}v(x,t)=F(x,t) & \textrm{in }\,\,Q,\cr v(x,0)=0,\quad\p_tv(x,0)=0 & \textrm{in }\,\,\M,\cr v(x,t)=0 & \textrm{on } \,\, \Sigma. \end{array} \right. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Homogeneous-boundary damped wave equation driven by an interior source $F$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction and main results

nodes.name: Lemma 1.1 (well-posedness and energy estimates for the damped wave equation with source)
nodes.statement_short: The source problem is well posed: a unique solution exists and satisfies first- and second-order energy estimates.

nodes.name: Lemma 1.2 (well-posedness of the Dirichlet problem and trace estimate)
nodes.statement_short: Dirichlet data $f\in H^1(\Sigma)$ vanishing at $t=0$ produce a unique solution whose normal derivative is $L^2(\Sigma)$-bounded by $\|f\|_{H^1}$.

nodes.name: Dirichlet to Neumann (D-N) map $\Lambda_{a,q}$
nodes.statement: We may define the Dirichlet to Neumann (D-N) map associated with hyperbolic problem (\ref{1.1}) by \begin{equation} \Lambda_{a,q}(f)=\p_\nu u,\quad f\in \mathcal{H}_0^{1}(\Sigma)=\set{f\in H^1(\Sigma),\,\, f(\cdot,0)=0\,\textrm{on}\,\,\p\M}. \end{equation} Therefore the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_{a,q}$ defined by (\ref{1.9}) is continuous. We denote by $\norm{\Lambda_{a,q}}$ its norm in $ \mathscr{L}\para{\mathcal{H}_0^1(\Sigma);L^2(\Sigma)}$.
nodes.statement_short: The measurement operator sending Dirichlet data $f$ to the Neumann trace $\p_\nu u$ of the corresponding solution.

nodes.name: Definition 1.3 (simple Riemannian manifold)
nodes.statement: We say that the Riemannian manifold $(\M,\g)$ (or that the metric $\g$) is simple in $\M$, if $\p \M$ is strictly convex with respect to $\g$, and for any $x\in \M$, the exponential map $\exp_x:\exp_x^{-1}(\M)\To \M$ is a diffeomorphism. The latter means that every two points $x; y \in \M$ are joined by a unique geodesic smoothly depending on $x$ and $y$.

nodes.name: Extension of a simple manifold to a larger simple manifold $\M_1$
nodes.statement: Note that if $(\M,\g)$ is simple, one can extend it to a simple manifold $\M_{1}$ such that $\M_1^{\textrm{int}}\supset\M$.

nodes.name: Admissible sets $\mathscr{A}(m_1,\eta)$ and $\mathscr{Q}(m_2)$ of coefficients
nodes.statement: Let us now introduce the admissible sets of absorption coefficients $a$ and electric potentials $q$. Let $m_1,m_2>0$ and $\eta> n/2$ be given, set \begin{equation} \mathscr{A}(m_1,\eta)= \set{a\in W^{2,\infty}(\M),\,\,\norm{a}_{H^\eta(\M)}\leq m_1}, \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \mathscr{Q}(m_2)= \set{q\in W^{2,\infty}(\M),\,\,\norm{q}_{H^2(\M)}\leq m_2}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: A priori bounded classes of $W^{2,\infty}$ absorption coefficients and potentials.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction and main results
nodes.definiendum: the admissible sets of absorption coefficients $a$ and electric potentials $q$

nodes.name: Curvature characteristic $k^+(\M,\g)$ (introduction)
nodes.statement: Introduce one more notation. Given $x\in\M$ and a 2-plane $\pi\subset T_x\M$, denote by $K(x,\pi)$ the sectional curvature of $\pi$ at $x$. For $\xi\in T_x\M$ with $\abs{\xi}=1$, put $$ K(x,\xi)=\sup_{\pi,\,\xi\in\pi}\,K(x,\pi),\quad K^+(x,\xi)=\max\{0,K(x,\xi)\}. $$ Define the following characteristic: $$ k^+(\M,\g)=\sup_\gamma\int_{\ell_1}^{\ell_2}tK^+(\gamma(t),\dot{\gamma}(t))dt, $$ where $\gamma\,:\,[\ell_1,\ell_2]\to\M$, ranges in the set of all unit speed geodesic in $\M$.
nodes.statement_short: Weighted supremum along geodesics of the positive part of the sectional curvature.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction and main results

nodes.name: Theorem 1.4 (Holder stability for the simultaneous determination of $a$ and $q$)
nodes.statement:
Let $(\M,\g)$ be a simple compact Riemannian manifold with boundary of dimension $n \geq 2$ such that $k^+(\M,\g)<1$, and let $T>	extrm{Diam}_\g(\M)$. There exist $C>0$ and $\gamma\in(0,1)$ such that for any $a_1,a_2\in\mathscr{A}(m_1,\eta)$ and $q_1,q_2\in\mathscr{Q}(m_2)$ coincide near the boundary $\p\M$, the following estimate holds true  egin{equation} 
orm{a_1-a_2}_{L^2(\M)}+
orm{q_1-q_2}_{L^2(\M)}\leq C
orm{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}^\gamma \end{equation} where $C$ depends on $\M$, $m_1,m_2$, $\eta$ and $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Main result: $\|a_1-a_2\|_{L^2}+\|q_1-q_2\|_{L^2}\le C\|\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}\|^\gamma$ on a simple manifold with $k^+<1$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction and main results
assumptions: Let $(\M,\g)$ be a simple compact Riemannian manifold with boundary of dimension $n \geq 2$ such that $k^+(\M,\g)<1$
for any $a_1,a_2\in\mathscr{A}(m_1,\eta)$ and $q_1,q_2\in\mathscr{Q}(m_2)$ coincide near the boundary $\p\M$

nodes.name: Corollary 1.5 (uniqueness from the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map)
nodes.statement: Let $(\M,\g)$ be a simple compact Riemannian manifold with boundary of dimension $n \geq 2$, such that $k^+(\M,\g)<1$ and let $T>\textrm{Diam}_\g(\M)$, we have that $\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}=\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}$ implies $a_1 =a_2$ and $q_1=q_2$ almost everywhere in $\M$.
nodes.statement_short: Equal D-N maps force $a_1=a_2$ and $q_1=q_2$ a.e.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction and main results
assumptions: Let $(\M,\g)$ be a simple compact Riemannian manifold with boundary of dimension $n \geq 2$, such that $k^+(\M,\g)<1$

nodes.name: Rakesh and Symes uniqueness for the time-independent potential
nodes.statement: In \cite{[Rakesh-Symes]}, Rakesh and Symes prove that the D-to-N map determines uniquely the time-independent potential in a wave equation.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction and main results
conclusions: the D-to-N map determines uniquely the time-independent potential in a wave equation.

nodes.name: Ramm and Sjostrand extension to time-dependent potentials
nodes.statement: Ramm and Sj\"ostrand \cite{[Ramm-Sjostrand]} has extended the result in \cite{[Rakesh-Symes]} to the case of time-dependent potentials.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction and main results
conclusions: has extended the result in \cite{[Rakesh-Symes]} to the case of time-dependent potentials

nodes.name: Sun stability estimates for potentials in the Euclidean case
nodes.statement: For the stability estimates, Sun \cite{[Sun]} established in the Euclidean case stability estimates for potentials from the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction and main results
conclusions: established in the Euclidean case stability estimates for potentials from the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map

nodes.name: Log-type stability from a partial Dirichlet-to-Neumann map
nodes.statement: In \cite{[BCY]} the authors consider the stability in an inverse problem of determining the potential $q$ entering the wave equation in a bounded smooth domain of $\R^d$ from boundary observations. The observation is given by a hyperbolic (dynamic) Dirichlet to Neumann map associated to a wave equation and prove a $\log$-type stability estimate in determining $q$ from a partial Dirichlet to Neumann map.
nodes.statement_short: A partial hyperbolic D-N map determines the potential $q$ with logarithmic stability.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction and main results
assumptions: the stability in an inverse problem of determining the potential $q$ entering the wave equation in a bounded smooth domain of $\R^d$ from boundary observations
The observation is given by a hyperbolic (dynamic) Dirichlet to Neumann map associated to a wave equation
conclusions: prove a $\log$-type stability estimate in determining $q$ from a partial Dirichlet to Neumann map

nodes.name: Bellassoued and Dos Santos Ferreira Holder stability for the potential
nodes.statement: In the case of Riemannian wave equation, Bellassoued and Dos Santos Ferriera \cite{[BellDSSF]} seek stability estimates in the inverse problem of determining the potential or the velocity in a wave equation posed in a simple riemannian wave equation $(\M,\g)$ from measured Neumann boundary observations. The authors prove in dimension $n\geq 2$ that the knowledge of the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map for the wave equation uniquely determines the electric potential and they show a Hölder-type stability in determining the potential. Similar results for the determination of velocities close to $1$ is also given.
nodes.statement_short: On a simple Riemannian manifold the D-N map determines the electric potential with Holder stability.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction and main results
assumptions: stability estimates in the inverse problem of determining the potential or the velocity in a wave equation posed in a simple riemannian wave equation $(\M,\g)$ from measured Neumann boundary observations
conclusions: The authors prove in dimension $n\geq 2$ that the knowledge of the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map for the wave equation uniquely determines the electric potential

nodes.name: Stefanov and Uhlmann conditional stability for the metric
nodes.statement: In \cite{[SU]} and \cite{[SU2]} Stefanov and Uhlmann considered the inverse problem of determining a Riemannian metric $\g$ on a Riemannian manifold $(\M,\g)$ with boundary from the hyperbolic Dirichlet-to-Neumann map associated to solutions of the wave equation $(\p_t^2-\Delta_\g)u=0$. A H\"older type of conditional stability estimate was proven in \cite{[SU]} for metrics close enough to the Euclidean metric in $\mathcal{C}^k$, $k\geq 1$ or for generic simple metrics in \cite{[SU2]}.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction and main results
assumptions: for metrics close enough to the Euclidean metric in $\mathcal{C}^k$, $k\geq 1$ or for generic simple metrics in \cite{[SU2]}
conclusions: A H\"older type of conditional stability estimate was proven in \cite{[SU]} for metrics close enough to the Euclidean metric in $\mathcal{C}^k$, $k\geq 1$ or for generic simple metrics in \cite{[SU2]}.

nodes.name: Gauge invariance of the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map
nodes.statement: It is clear that one cannot hope to uniquely determine the metric $\g=(\g_{jk})$ from the knowledge of the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_{\g,a,\,q}$. As was noted in \cite{[SU]}, the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map is invariant under a gauge transformation of the metric~$\g$. Namely, given a diffeomorphism $\psi:\M\to \M$ such that $\psi|_{\p\M}={\rm Id}$ one has $\Lambda_{\psi^*\g,a,\,q}=\Lambda_{\g,a,\,q}$ where $\psi^*\g$ denotes the pullback of the metric $\g$ under $\psi$.
nodes.statement_short: $\Lambda_{\psi^*\g,a,q}=\Lambda_{\g,a,q}$ for any boundary-fixing diffeomorphism $\psi$, so the metric is only determined up to gauge.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction and main results
assumptions: given a diffeomorphism $\psi:\M\to \M$ such that $\psi|_{\p\M}={\rm Id}$
conclusions: one has $\Lambda_{\psi^*\g,a,\,q}=\Lambda_{\g,a,\,q}$ where $\psi^*\g$ denotes the pullback of the metric $\g$ under $\psi$.

nodes.name: Montalto simultaneous recovery of metric, covector field and potential
nodes.statement: In \cite{[Montalo]}, Montalto studies the stability of simultaneously recovering the Riemannian metric $\g$, a covector field $b$ and a potential $q$ in a Riemannian manifold $\M$ from the boundary measurements modeled by the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map. He shows that, assuming the metric is close to a generic simple metric, and the two covector close, a conditional H\"older-type stability for the recovery holds up to the natural gauge transformations that fix the boundary.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction and main results
assumptions: assuming the metric is close to a generic simple metric, and the two covector close
conclusions: a conditional H\"older-type stability for the recovery holds up to the natural gauge transformations that fix the boundary.

nodes.name: Belishev and Kurylev reconstruction of a smooth metric
nodes.statement: In \cite{[BK]} Belishev and Kurylev gave an affirmative answer to the general problem of finding a smooth metric from the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction and main results
conclusions: gave an affirmative answer to the general problem of finding a smooth metric from the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map.

nodes.name: Sphere bundle $S\M$ and co-sphere bundle $S^*\M$
nodes.statement: Let $(\M,\g)$ be a Riemannian manifold, for $x\in \M$ and $\xi\in T_x\M$ we let $\gamma_{x,\xi}$ denote the unique geodesic starting at the point $x$ in the direction $\xi$. By \begin{align*} S\M=\set{(x,\xi)\in T\M;\,\abs{\xi}=1}, \quad S^*\M=\set{(x,p)\in T^*\M;\,\abs{p}=1}, \end{align*} we denote the sphere bundle and co-sphere bundle of $\M$.
nodes.section: 2 Stability estimate for the geodesical $X$-ray transform
nodes.definiendum: the sphere bundle and co-sphere bundle of $\M$

nodes.name: Exponential map $\exp_x$
nodes.statement: The exponential map $\exp_x:T_x\M\to \M$ is given by \begin{equation} \exp_x(v)=\gamma_{x,\xi}(\abs{v}),\quad \xi=\frac{v\,\,}{\abs{v}}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2 Stability estimate for the geodesical $X$-ray transform

nodes.name: Convex non-trapping manifold
nodes.statement: A compact Riemannian manifold $(\M,\, \g)$ with boundary is called a convex non-trapping manifold, if it satisfies two conditions: \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] the boundary $\p \M$ is strictly convex, i.e., the second fundamental form of the boundary is positive definite at every boundary point, \item[(ii)] all geodesics having finite length in $\M$, i.e., for each $(x,\xi) \in S\M$, the maximal geodesic $\gamma_{x,\xi}(t)$ satisfying the initial conditions $\gamma_{x,\xi}(0) = x$ and $\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(0) = \xi$ is defined on a finite segment with extremities $\ell_{-}(x,\xi)$ and $\ell_{+}(x,\xi)$. We recall that a geodesic $\gamma: [a, b] \To M$ is maximal if it cannot be extended to a segment $[a-\varepsilon_1, b+\varepsilon_2]$, where $\varepsilon_i \geq 0$ and $\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 > 0$.
nodes.statement_short: A compact manifold with strictly convex boundary all of whose maximal geodesics have finite length.
nodes.section: 2 Stability estimate for the geodesical $X$-ray transform
nodes.genus: A compact Riemannian manifold $(\M,\, \g)$ with boundary
differentia: the boundary $\p \M$ is strictly convex, i.e., the second fundamental form of the boundary is positive definite at every boundary point
all geodesics having finite length in $\M$

nodes.name: Simple manifold (convex, non-trapping, no conjugate points)
nodes.statement: An important subclass of convex non-trapping manifolds are simple manifolds. We say that a compact Riemannian manifold $(\M, \g)$ is simple if it satisfies the following properties \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] $(\M,\g)$ is convex and non-trapping, \item[(b)] there are no conjugate points on any geodesic.
nodes.section: 2 Stability estimate for the geodesical $X$-ray transform
differentia: there are no conjugate points on any geodesic

nodes.name: A simple manifold is diffeomorphic to a closed ball
nodes.statement: A simple $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold is diffeomorphic to a closed ball in $\R^n$, and any pair of points in the manifold are joined by an unique geodesic.
nodes.section: 2 Stability estimate for the geodesical $X$-ray transform
conclusions: A simple $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold is diffeomorphic to a closed ball in $\R^n$, and any pair of points in the manifold are joined by an unique geodesic.

nodes.name: Geodesic flow $\phi_t$ on $S\M$
nodes.statement: Let $(x,\xi)\in S\M$, there exist a unique geodesic $\gamma_{x,\xi}$ associated to $(x,\xi)$ which is maxmimally defined on a finite intervall $[\ell_-(x,\xi),\ell_+(x,\xi)]$, with $\gamma_{x,\xi}(\ell_\pm(x,\xi))\in\p\M$. We define the geodesic flow $\phi_t$ as following \begin{equation} \phi_t:S\M\to S\M,\quad \phi_t(x,\xi)=(\gamma_{x,\xi}(t),\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(t)),\quad t\in [\ell_-(x,\xi),\ell_+(x,\xi)], \end{equation} and $\phi_t$ is a flow, that is, $\phi_t\circ\phi_s=\phi_{t+s}$.
nodes.section: 2 Stability estimate for the geodesical $X$-ray transform

nodes.name: Submanifolds $\p_\pm S\M$ of inner and outer vectors
nodes.statement: Now, we introduce the submanifolds of inner and outer vectors of $S\M$ \begin{equation} \p_{\pm}S\M =\set{(x,\xi)\in S\M,\, x \in \p \M,\, \pm\seq{\xi,\nu(x)}< 0}, \end{equation} where $\nu$ is the unit outer normal to the boundary. Note that the manifolds $\p_+ S\M$ and $\p_-S\M$ have the same boundary $S(\p \M)$, and $\p S\M = \p_+ S\M\cup \p_- S\M$.
nodes.section: 2 Stability estimate for the geodesical $X$-ray transform
nodes.definiendum: the submanifolds of inner and outer vectors of $S\M$

nodes.name: Properties of the travel time functions $\ell_\pm$
nodes.statement: Thus we can define two functions $\ell_\pm:S\M\to\R$ which satisfy $$ \ell_-(x,\xi)\leq 0,\quad \ell_+(x,\xi)\geq 0,\quad \ell_+(x,\xi)=-\ell_-(x,-\xi), $$ $$ \ell_-(x,\xi)=0,\quad (x,\xi)\in\p_+S\M,\quad \ell_+(x,\xi)=0,\quad (x,\xi)\in\p_-S\M, $$ $$ \ell_-(\phi_t(x,\xi))=\ell_-(x,\xi)-t,\quad \ell_+(\phi_t(x,\xi))=\ell_+(x,\xi)-t.
nodes.statement_short: The exit and entry times satisfy sign, symmetry, boundary-vanishing and cocycle relations along the flow.
nodes.section: 2 Stability estimate for the geodesical $X$-ray transform

nodes.name: Smoothness of $\ell_\pm$ away from $T(\p\M)$
nodes.statement: Concerning smoothness properties of $\ell_{\pm}(x,\xi)$, we can see that these functions are smooth near a point $(x,\xi)$ such that the geodesic $\gamma_{x,\xi}(t)$ intersects $\p\M$ transversely for $t=\ell_{\pm}(x,\xi)$. By strict convexity of $\p\M$, the functions $\ell_{\pm}(x,\xi)$ are smooth on $T\M \setminus T(\p\M).$ In fact, all points of $T\M \cap T(\p\M)$ are singular for $\ell_{\pm}$; since some derivatives of these functions are unbounded in a neighbourhood of such points. In particular, $\ell_{+}$ is smooth on $\p_+SM$, see Lemma 4.1.1 of \cite{[Sh]}.
nodes.statement_short: Strict convexity makes $\ell_\pm$ smooth on $T\M\setminus T(\p\M)$, and $\ell_+$ smooth on $\p_+S\M$.
nodes.section: 2 Stability estimate for the geodesical $X$-ray transform
conclusions: the functions $\ell_{\pm}(x,\xi)$ are smooth on $T\M \setminus T(\p\M).$

nodes.name: Volume form $\dd\omega_x(\xi)$ on $S_x\M$
nodes.statement: The Riemannian scalar product on $T_x\M$ induces the volume form on $S_x\M$, denoted by $\dd \omega_x(\xi)$ and given by $$ \dd \omega_x(\xi)=\sqrt{\abs{\g}} \, \sum_{k=1}^n(-1)^k\xi^k \dd \xi^1\wedge\cdots\wedge \widehat{\dd \xi^k}\wedge\cdots\wedge \dd \xi^n. $$ As usual, the notation $\, \widehat{\cdot} \,$ means that the corresponding factor has been dropped.
nodes.section: 2 Stability estimate for the geodesical $X$-ray transform

nodes.name: Volume forms $\dvv$ on $S\M$ and $\dss$ on $\p S\M$
nodes.statement: We introduce the volume form $\dvv$ on the manifold $S\M$ by $$ \dvv (x,\xi)=\dd\omega_x(\xi)\wedge \dv, $$ where $\dv$ is the Riemannnian volume form on $\M$. By Liouville's theorem, the form $\dvv$ is preserved by the geodesic flow. The corresponding volume form on the boundary $\p S\M =\set{(x,\xi)\in S\M,\, x\in\p \M}$ is given by $$ \dss=\dd\omega_x(\xi) \wedge \ds, $$ where $\ds$ is the volume form of $\p \M$.
nodes.statement_short: Liouville volume on the sphere bundle and its boundary analogue, preserved by the geodesic flow.
nodes.section: 2 Stability estimate for the geodesical $X$-ray transform

nodes.name: The weighted space $L^2_\mu(\p_+S\M)$
nodes.statement: Let $L^2_\mu(\p_+S\M)$ be the space of square integrable functions with respect to the measure $\mu(x,\xi)\dss$ with $\mu(x,\xi)=\abs{\seq{\xi,\nu(x)}}$. This Hilbert space is endowed with the scalar product \begin{equation} \para{u,v}_\mu=\int_{\p_+S\M}u(x,\xi) \overline{v}(x,\xi) \mu(x,\xi)\dss. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2 Stability estimate for the geodesical $X$-ray transform
nodes.genus: the space of square integrable functions
differentia: with respect to the measure $\mu(x,\xi)\dss$ with $\mu(x,\xi)=\abs{\seq{\xi,\nu(x)}}$

nodes.name: Geodesic $X$-ray (ray) transform $\I$
nodes.statement: The ray transform (also called geodesic $X$-ray transform) on a convex non trapping manifold $\M$ is the linear operator \begin{equation} \I:\mathcal{C}^\infty(\M)\To \mathcal{C}^\infty(\p_+S\M), \end{equation} defined by the equality \begin{equation} \I f(x,\xi)=\int_0^{\ell_+(x,\xi)}f(\gamma_{x,\xi}(t))\, \dd t,\quad (x,\xi)\in\p_+S\M. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\I f(x,\xi)$ integrates $f$ along the maximal geodesic issued from the inward boundary vector $(x,\xi)$.
nodes.section: 2 Stability estimate for the geodesical $X$-ray transform
nodes.definiendum: The ray transform (also called geodesic $X$-ray transform)

nodes.name: Smoothness of $\I f$ on $\p_+S\M$
nodes.statement: The right-hand side of (\ref{2.6}) is a smooth function on $\p_+S\M$ because the integration limit $\ell_+(x,\xi)$ is a smooth function on $\p_+S\M$.
nodes.section: 2 Stability estimate for the geodesical $X$-ray transform

nodes.name: Boundedness of the ray transform on $H^k$
nodes.statement: The ray transform on a convex non trapping manifold $\M$ can be extended as a bounded operator \begin{equation} \I:H^k(\M)\To H^k(\p_+S\M), \end{equation} for every integer $k\geq 1$, see Theorem 4.2.1 of \cite{[Sh]}.
nodes.statement_short: $\I$ extends to a bounded operator $H^k(\M)\to H^k(\p_+S\M)$ for every $k\ge1$.
nodes.section: 2 Stability estimate for the geodesical $X$-ray transform
conclusions: The ray transform on a convex non trapping manifold $\M$ can be extended as a bounded operator \begin{equation} \I:H^k(\M)\To H^k(\p_+S\M),

Let $R$ be the curvature tensor of the Levi-Civita connection $

nodes.name: Sectional curvature $K(x,\pi)$
nodes.statement: For a point $x \in \M$ and a two-dimensional subspace $\pi \subset T_x\M,$ the number $$ K(x,\pi)=\frac{\langle R(\xi,\eta)\eta,\xi\rangle}{\vert \xi \vert^2 \vert \eta \vert^2-\langle \xi, \eta \rangle^2}, $$ is independent of the choice of the basis $\xi$, $\eta$ for $\pi$. It is called the sectional curvature of the manifold $\M$ at the point $x$ and in the two-dimentional direction $\pi$.

nodes.definiendum: the sectional curvature of the manifold $\M$ at the point $x$ and in the two-dimentional direction $\pi$

nodes.name: The curvature quantities $K^+(x,\xi)$ and $k^+(\M,\g)$
nodes.statement: For $(x,\xi)\in T\M$, we set $K(x,\xi)=\underset{\pi \ni \xi}{\sup} K(x,\pi) $ and \begin{equation} K^+(x,\xi)=\max\{0,K(x,\xi)\}. \end{equation} For a simple compact Riemannian manifold $(\M,\g)$, we set \begin{equation} k^+(\M,\g)=\sup\lbrace \int_0^{\ell_+(x,\xi)} tK^+(\gamma_{x,\xi}(t),\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(t)) dt, \; (x,\xi)\in \p_+S\M\rbrace. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $k^+$ is the supremum over inward boundary directions of $\int_0^{\ell_+} tK^+\,dt$ along the geodesic.
nodes.section: 2 Stability estimate for the geodesical $X$-ray transform

nodes.name: Theorem 2.1 (stability estimate for the geodesic $X$-ray transform)
nodes.statement: For every simple compact Riemannian manifold $(\M,\g)$ with $k^+(\M,\g)<1$, there exist $C>0$ such that the following stability estimate \begin{equation} \Vert f \Vert _{L^2(\M)}\leq C \Vert \I f \Vert_{H^1(\p_+S\M)}, \end{equation} holds for any $f\in H^1(\M)$.
nodes.statement_short: If $k^+<1$ then $\|f\|_{L^2(\M)}\le C\|\I f\|_{H^1(\p_+S\M)}$: the ray transform is stably invertible.
nodes.section: 2 Stability estimate for the geodesical $X$-ray transform
assumptions: For every simple compact Riemannian manifold $(\M,\g)$ with $k^+(\M,\g)<1$

nodes.name: Reduction to smooth $f$ by density
nodes.statement: By density arguments, it suffices to prove the theorem for $f \in \mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\M)$. Indeed, if $f\in H^1(M)$, then we can find a sequence $(f_k)_k$ in $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\M)$ converging towards $f$ in $H^1(\M).$ The ray transform $\I$ is a bounded operator from $H^1(\M)$ into $H^1(\p_+S\M)$, so the sequence $(\I f_k)_k$ converges towards $\I f$ in $H^1(\p_+S\M).$ Applying the theorem for $f_k$ and passing to the limit as $k \rightarrow +\infty,$ we deduce that $ \Vert f \Vert _{L^2(\M)}\leq C \Vert \I f \Vert_{H^1(\p_+S\M)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Approximating $f\in H^1$ by smooth functions and using boundedness of $\I$ reduces Theorem 2.1 to the smooth case.

nodes.name: Einstein summation convention
nodes.statement: We will use the Einstein summation convention to abbreviate the notations. When an index variable appears twice in a simple term and is not otherwise defined, it implies summation of that term over all the values of the index. For example, for $i\in{1,2,3}$, $c_ix^i$ means $c_1x^1+c_2x^2+c_3x^3$.

nodes.name: Tensor fields of degree $(r,s)$ and the modules $\mathcal{C}^\infty(\tau_s^r\M,U)$
nodes.statement: Let $\tau_s^r\M$ be the bundle of tensors of degree $(r,s)$ on $\M$. Its sections denoted by $T_s^r$ are called \textit{tensor fields of degree $(r,s)$.} Let $U$ be a domain of $\M $. We denote by $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\tau_s^r\M,U)$ the $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(U)$-module of smooth sections of the bundle $\tau_s^r \M$ over $U$. The notation $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\tau_s^r\M,\M)$ will usually be abbreviated to $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\tau_s^r\M).$

nodes.name: Coordinates of a tensor field
nodes.statement: If $(x^1,\dots,x^n)$ is a local coordinate system defined in a domain $U$, then any tensor field $u\in \mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\tau_s^r \M,U)$ can be uniquely represented as \begin{equation} u=u_{j_1,\dots,j_s}^{i_1,\dots,i_r} \frac{\p}{\p x^{i_1}}\otimes\dots\otimes\frac{\p}{\p x^{i_r}}\otimes dx^{j_1} \otimes \dots \otimes dx^{j_s}, \end{equation} where $u_{j_1,\cdots,j_s}^{i_1,\cdots,i_r} \in \mathcal{C}^{\infty}(U)$ are called the coordinates of the field $u$ in the given coordinate system. We will usually abbreviate (\ref{2.11}) as follows \begin{equation} u=(u_{j_1,\cdots,j_s}^{i_1,\cdots,i_r}). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Natural coordinate systems on $T\M$ and semibasic tensors
nodes.statement: Now, we will extend this covariant differenciation for tensors on $T\M$. If $(x^1,\dots, x^n)$ is a local coordinate system defined in a domain $U \subset \M$, then we denote by $\frac{\p}{\p x^i}$ the coordinate vector fields and by $dx^i$ the coordinate covector fields. We recall that the coordinates of a vector $\xi \in T_x\M$ are the coefficients of the expansion $\xi=\xi^i \frac{\p}{\p x^i}$. Let $p$ be the projection on $\M$. On the domain $p^{-1}(U)\subset T\M$, the family of the functions $(x^1, \dots,x^n,\xi^1,\dots,\xi^n)$ is a local coordinate system which is called \textit{associated} with the system $(x^1,\dots,x^n).$ A local coordinate system on $T\M$ will be called a \textit{natural coordinate system} if it is associated with some local coordinate system on $\M$. In the sequel, we will use only such coordinate systems on $T\M$. The algebra of tensor fields of the manifold $T\M$ is generated locally by the coordinate fields $\frac{\p}{\p x^i},\frac{\p}{\p \xi^i}, dx^i, d\xi^i.$ A tensor $u \in T^r_{s,(x,\xi)}(T\M)$ of degree $(r,s)$ at a point $(x,\xi)\in T\M$ is called \textit{semibasic} if in some (and so, in any) natural coordinate system, it can be represented as: \begin{equation} u=u_{j_1 \dots j_s}^{i_1 \dots i_r} \frac{\p}{\p \xi^{i_1}}\otimes\dots\otimes\frac{\p}{\p \xi^{i_r}}\otimes dx^{j_1} \otimes \dots \otimes dx^{j_s}. \end{equation} We will abbreviate this equality to $$u=(u_{j_1 \dots j_s}^{i_1 \dots i_r} ).$$ We denote by $\beta_s^r\M$ the subbundle in $\tau_s^r(T\M)$ made of all semibasic tensors of degree $(r,s).$ Note that $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\beta_0^0 \M)=\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(T \M)$. The elements of $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\beta_0^1 \M)$ are called the \textit{semibasic vector fields}, and the elements of $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\beta_1^0 \M)$ are called \textit{semibasic covector fields}.
nodes.statement_short: Tensors on $T\M$ expanded in $\p/\p\xi^i\otimes dx^j$ only are called semibasic; they form the subbundle $\beta_s^r\M$.

nodes.name: Canonical imbedding $\iota$ of tensor fields into semibasic tensor fields

Thus we obtain the canonical imbedding \begin{equation} \iota:\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\tau_s^r \M) \subset \mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\beta_s^r \M). \end{equation} Note that $\iota( \frac{\p}{\p x^{i}})= \frac{\p}{\p \xi^{i}}$ and $\iota(dx^i)=dx^i.

nodes.statement: To prove Theorem \ref{theorem}, we also need the two following divergence formulas (see \cite{[Sh]}, p 101).\\ \textit{Gauss-Ostrogradskii formula} of the vertical divergence \begin{equation} \int_{S\M} \overset{\vv}{\dive}(W)\, \dvv=(n-2) \int_{S\M} \langle W,\xi\rangle \, \dvv,\quad W\in \mathcal{C}^\infty(T\M), \end{equation} \textit{Gauss-Ostrogradskii formula} of the horizontal divergence \begin{equation} \int_{S\M} \overset{\hh}{\dive}(V)\, \dvv= \int_{\p S\M} \langle V,\nu\rangle \, \dss, \quad V\in \mathcal{C}^\infty(T\M),

nodes.name: Geodesic vector field $H$ (differentiation along geodesics)
nodes.statement: Let $H$ denote the vector field associated with the geodesic flow $\phi_t$. For $u\in \mathcal{C}^\infty(S\M)$ and $(x,\xi)\in S\M$, we have \begin{equation} Hu(x,\xi)=\frac{d}{dt}u(\phi_t(x,\xi))_{|t=0}. \end{equation} and we call it the differentiation along the geodesics. In coordinate form, we have \begin{equation} H=\xi^i\frac{\p}{\p x^i}-\Gamma^i_{jk}\xi^j\xi^k\frac{\p}{\p \xi^i}=\xi^i (\frac{\p}{\p x^i}-\Gamma^p_{iq}\xi^q \frac{\p}{\p \xi^p})=\xi^i\overset{\hh}{\nabla}_i. \end{equation}

nodes.name: The ray-transform primitive $u(x,\xi)$ and its boundary conditions
nodes.statement: We introduce the function $u:S\M\to\R$ defined by \begin{equation} u(x,\xi)=\int_0^{\ell_+(x,\xi)}f(\gamma_{x,\xi}(t)) dt. \end{equation} It satisfies the boundary conditions \begin{equation} u=\I f,\quad\mbox{on }\p_+ S\M, \end{equation} and, since $\ell_+(x,\xi)=0$ for $(x,\xi)\in \p_- S\M$, we have \begin{equation} u=0,\quad\mbox{on }\p_- S\M. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $u$ integrates $f$ from $(x,\xi)$ to the exit point; it equals $\I f$ on $\p_+S\M$ and vanishes on $\p_-S\M$.

nodes.name: Lemma 2.2 (homogeneity and kinetic equations for $u$)
nodes.statement: The function $u$ given by (\ref{2.34}) is smooth on $T\M\backslash T(\p\M)$ and has the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item $u$ is homogeneous function of degree $-1$ in $\xi$. \item $u$ satisfies the following kinetic equation $Hu=-f$. \item $u$ satisfies the following equation $H\overset{\vv}{\nabla} u=-\overset{\hh}{\nabla} u$.

nodes.name: Homogeneity of degree $-1$ in $\xi$

Then $$ u(x,\lambda \xi)=\int_0^{\frac{1}{\lambda}\ell_+(x,\xi)}f(\gamma_{x,\xi}(\lambda t)) dt = \frac{1}{\lambda} u(x,\xi).

nodes.name: Kinetic equation $Hu=-f$
nodes.statement: Prove item (2). For $s \in \R$ sufficiently small, we set $x_s=\gamma_{x,\xi}(s)$ and $\xi_s=\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(s).$ Then, $\gamma_{x_s,\xi_s}(t)=\gamma_{x,\xi}(t+s)$ and $\ell_+(x_s,\xi_s)=\tau_+(x,\xi)-s.$ So, $$ u(\gamma_{x,\xi}(s),\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(s))=u(x_s,\xi_s) = \int_0^{\ell_+(x_s,\xi_s)}f(\gamma_{x,\xi}(t+s)) dt =\int_s^{\ell_+(x,\xi)}f(\gamma_{x,\xi}(t)) dt . $$ Differentiating with respect to $s$ and taking $s=0$, we obtain that $$ \frac{\p u}{\p x_i}\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}^i(0)+\frac{\p u}{\p \xi_i} \ddot {\gamma}_{x,\xi}^{i}(0)=-f(x). $$ Since we have $\gamma_{x,\xi}(0)=x$, $\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(0)=\xi$ and $\ddot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}^{i}(0)=-\Gamma ^i_{jk}(x)\xi^j\xi^k,$ then $$\xi^i\frac{\p u}{\p x_i}-\Gamma^i_{jk}\xi^j\xi^k\frac{\p u}{\p \xi_i}= -f(x).$$ Thus we have $Hu=-f$.

nodes.name: The WKB expansion method
nodes.statement: The WKB expansion method is a classical way to construct a special solution with a large parameter of wave systems. It is based on the assumption that the solution of the wave equation, can be sought as an expansion in powers of the frequency. This expansion arises here as a power series depending on the small parameter $h$, which represents the relative wavelength of the initial conditions. Introducing it in a scalar wave equation leads to a system of coupled equations governing the behavior of the phase (eikonal equation) and of the amplitudes of the different expansion coefficients (transport equations).

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement: By the simplicity assumption, since $y\notin\overline{\M}$, we have $\varrho\in\mathcal{C}^\infty(\M)$, and in polar normal coordinates, we get \begin{equation} \widetilde{\varrho}(r,\xi)=r=d_\g(y,x). \end{equation} The proof is complete.
nodes.statement_short: In polar normal coordinates $\widetilde\varrho(r,\xi)=r$, so the eikonal equation is immediate from simplicity.
nodes.section: 3 Geometric optics solutions for the damped wave equation

nodes.name: The solution spaces $\mathcal{V}(Q)$ and $\mathcal{W}(Q)$
nodes.statement:
Let us introduce the following spaces:  egin{equation} \mathcal{V}(Q)=\set{	heta\in H^3(0,T;L^2(\M))\cap H^1(0,T;H^2(\M)),\,\,\p_t^j	heta(\cdot,0)=\p_t^j	heta(\cdot,T)=0,\,j=0,1,2.}, \end{equation} and  egin{equation} \mathcal{W}(Q)=\set{\psi\in W^{2,\infty}(Q),\,\, \p_t\psi\in W^{2,\infty}(Q)}, \end{equation} equipped with the norms:  egin{eqnarray*} 
orm{	heta}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}&:=&
orm{	heta}_{H^1(0,T;H^2(\M))}+
orm{	heta}_{H^3(0,T;L^2(\M))}, \quad 	heta\in\mathcal{V}(Q),\cr \ 
orm{\psi}_{\mathcal{W}(Q)}&:=&
orm{\psi}_{W^{2,\infty}(Q)}+
orm{\p_t\psi}_{W^{2,\infty}(Q)},\quad \psi\in\mathcal{W}(Q). \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Amplitude spaces: $\mathcal{V}(Q)$ of time-regular functions vanishing to second order at $t=0,T$, and $\mathcal{W}(Q)\subset W^{2,\infty}$.
nodes.section: 3 Geometric optics solutions for the damped wave equation

nodes.name: First transport equation
nodes.statement: We want to find a function $\theta\in \mathcal{V}(Q)$ which solves the first transport equation \begin{equation} \p_t \theta+\seq{d\varrho,d\theta}+\frac{1}{2} (\Delta \varrho)\theta=0,\qquad \forall t\in\R,\, x\in\M, \end{equation} where $\varrho$ is given by Lemma \ref{L.3.1}.
nodes.statement_short: $\p_t\theta+\langle d\varrho,d\theta\rangle+\frac12(\Delta\varrho)\theta=0$ for the principal amplitude.
nodes.section: 3 Geometric optics solutions for the damped wave equation

nodes.name: Second transport equation (absorption amplitude)
nodes.statement: Moreover for $a\in W^{2,\infty}(\M) $, we need to find a function $\psi_a\in\mathcal{W}(Q) $ which solves the second transport equation \begin{equation} \p_t \psi_a+\seq{d\varrho,d\psi_a}+\frac{a}{2}\psi_a=0,\qquad \forall t\in\R,\, x\in\M. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\p_t\psi_a+\langle d\varrho,d\psi_a\rangle+\frac a2\psi_a=0$, the equation carrying the absorption coefficient.
nodes.section: 3 Geometric optics solutions for the damped wave equation

nodes.name: Laplacian of a radial function in geodesic polar coordinates
nodes.statement: Recall that if $f(r)$ is any function of the geodesic distance $r$, then \begin{equation} \Delta_{\widetilde{\g}}f(r)=f''(r)+\frac{\alpha^{-1}}{2}\frac{\p \alpha}{\p r}f'(r). \end{equation} Here $\alpha=\alpha(r,\xi)$ denotes the square of the volume element in geodesic polar coordinates.
nodes.statement_short: $\Delta_{\widetilde\g}f(r)=f''(r)+\frac{\alpha^{-1}}2\frac{\p\alpha}{\p r}f'(r)$ with $\alpha$ the squared volume element.
nodes.section: 3 Geometric optics solutions for the damped wave equation
assumptions: if $f(r)$ is any function of the geodesic distance $r$

nodes.name: Explicit solution of the first transport equation
nodes.statement: The transport equation (\ref{3.11}) becomes \begin{equation} \frac{\p \widetilde{\theta}}{\p t}+\frac{\p \widetilde{\varrho}}{\p r}\frac{\p \widetilde{\theta}}{\p r}+\frac{1}{4}\widetilde{\theta}\alpha^{-1}\frac{\p \alpha}{\p r}\frac{\p \widetilde{\varrho}}{\p r}=0. \end{equation} Thus $\widetilde{\theta}$ satisfies \begin{equation} \frac{\p \widetilde{\theta}}{\p t}+\frac{\p \widetilde{\theta}}{\p r}+\frac{1}{4}\widetilde{\theta}\alpha^{-1}\frac{\p \alpha}{\p r}=0. \end{equation} Let $\phi\in\mathcal{C}_0^\infty(\R)$ and $\Psi\in H^2(S^+_y\M)$. Let us write $\widetilde{\theta}$ in the form \begin{equation} \widetilde{\theta}(t,r,\xi)=\alpha^{-1/4}\phi(t-r)\Psi(\xi). \end{equation} Direct computations yield \begin{equation} \frac{\p \widetilde{\theta}}{\p t}(t,r,\xi)=\alpha^{-1/4}\phi'(t-r)\Psi(\xi), \end{equation} and, we find \begin{equation} \frac{\p \widetilde{\theta}}{\p r}(t,r,\xi)=-\frac{1}{4}\alpha^{-5/4}\frac{\p\alpha}{\p r}\phi(t-r)\Psi(\xi)-\alpha^{-1/4}\phi'(t-r)\Psi(\xi). \end{equation} Finally, (\ref{3.18}) and (\ref{3.17}) yield \begin{equation} \frac{\p \widetilde{\theta}}{\p t}(t,r,\xi)+\frac{\p \widetilde{\theta}}{\p r}(t,r,\xi)=-\frac{1}{4}\alpha^{-1}\widetilde{\theta}(t,r,\xi)\frac{\p\alpha}{\p r}. \end{equation} Now if we assume that $\mathrm{supp}(\phi) \subset (0,\epsilon)$, then for any $x=\exp_y(r\xi)\in \M$, it is easy to see that $$ \p_t^j\widetilde{\theta}(0,r,\xi)=\p_t^j\widetilde{\theta}(T,r,\xi)=0,\quad j=0,1,2,\,\, T-r>\varepsilon.
nodes.statement_short: The ansatz $\widetilde\theta=\alpha^{-1/4}\phi(t-r)\Psi(\xi)$ solves the first transport equation and vanishes to second order at $t=0$ and $t=T$.
nodes.section: 3 Geometric optics solutions for the damped wave equation

nodes.name: Explicit solution of the second transport equation
nodes.statement: For the second transport equation (\ref{3.12}), in polar coordinates, takes the form \begin{equation} \frac{\p \widetilde{\psi}_a}{\p t}+\frac{\p \widetilde{\varrho}}{\p r}\frac{\p \widetilde{\psi}_a}{\p r} +\frac{1}{2}\widetilde{a}(r,y,\xi)\widetilde{\psi}_a=0, \end{equation} where $\widetilde{a}(r,y,\xi):=a(\theta_r(y,\xi))$. Thus $\widetilde{\psi}_a$ satisfies \begin{equation} \frac{\p \widetilde{\psi}_a}{\p t}+\frac{\p \widetilde{\psi}_a}{\p r}+\frac{1}{2}\widetilde{a}(r,y,\xi)\widetilde{\psi}_a=0. \end{equation} Thus, we can choose $\widetilde{\psi}_a$ as following \begin{equation} \widetilde{\psi}_a(t,y,r,\xi)=\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^t\widetilde{a}(r-s,y,\xi)ds}. \end{equation} Since $a\in W^{2,\infty}(\M)$, we get $\psi_a\in \mathcal{W}(Q)$. Hence (\ref{3.12}) is solved.
nodes.statement_short: $\widetilde\psi_a=\exp(-\frac12\int_0^t\widetilde a(r-s,y,\xi)ds)$ solves the second transport equation and lies in $\mathcal{W}(Q)$.
nodes.section: 3 Geometric optics solutions for the damped wave equation
conclusions: Thus, we can choose $\widetilde{\psi}_a$ as following \begin{equation} \widetilde{\psi}_a(t,y,r,\xi)=\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^t\widetilde{a}(r-s,y,\xi)ds}. \end{equation} Since $a\in W^{2,\infty}(\M)$, we get $\psi_a\in \mathcal{W}(Q)$. Hence (\ref{3.12}) is solved.

nodes.name: Phase function $\varphi(x,t)=\varrho(x)-t$
nodes.statement: We introduce the function \begin{equation} \varphi(x,t):=\varrho(x)-t,\quad x\in\M,\,\, t\in (0,T), \end{equation} where $\varrho$ is given by Lemma \ref{L.3.1}.
nodes.section: 3 Geometric optics solutions for the damped wave equation

nodes.name: Lemma 3.2 (geometric optics solutions of the damped wave equation)
nodes.statement: Let $a\in W^{2,\infty}(\M)$, $q\in W^{2,\infty}(\M)$, and $\theta\in\mathcal{V}(Q)$, $\psi_{a}\in\mathcal{W}(Q)$ solve respectively (\ref{3.11}) and (\ref{3.12}). Then for all $h>0$ small enough, there exists a solution $$ u(x,t;h)\in \mathcal{C}^2(0,T;L^2(\M))\cap\mathcal{C}^1(0,T;H^1(\M))\cap\mathcal{C}(0,T;H^2(\M)) $$ of the wave equation \begin{equation*} (\p^2_t-\Op)u=0,\quad \textrm{in}\quad Q, \end{equation*} with the initial condition \begin{equation*} u(x,0)=\p_tu(x,0)=0,\quad \textrm{in}\quad \M, \end{equation*} of the form \begin{equation} u(x,t)=\theta(x,t)\psi_a(x,t)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}+r_h(x,t), \end{equation} the remainder $r_h(x,t)$ is such that \begin{align*} r_h(x,t)&=0,\quad (x,t)\in \Sigma , \\ r_h(x,0)=\p_t r_h(x,0)&=0,\quad x\in \M. \end{align*} Furthermore, there exist $C>0$, $h_0>0$ such that, for all $h \leq h_0$ the following estimates hold true. \begin{equation} \sum_{k=0}^2 \sum_{j=0}^{k} h^{k-1} \|\p_t^{j} r_h(\cdot,t)\|_{H^{k-j}(\M)}\leq C\norm{\theta}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}. \end{equation} The constant $C$ depends only on $T$ and $\M$ (that is $C$ does not depend on $a$ and $h$).
nodes.statement_short: For small $h$ there is a forward solution $u=\theta\psi_a e^{i\varphi/h}+r_h$ with a remainder controlled by $h\|\theta\|_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}$.
nodes.section: 3 Geometric optics solutions for the damped wave equation
assumptions: Let $a\in W^{2,\infty}(\M)$, $q\in W^{2,\infty}(\M)$, and $\theta\in\mathcal{V}(Q)$, $\psi_{a}\in\mathcal{W}(Q)$ solve respectively (\ref{3.11}) and (\ref{3.12})
conclusions: there exists a solution $$ u(x,t;h)\in \mathcal{C}^2(0,T;L^2(\M))\cap\mathcal{C}^1(0,T;H^1(\M))\cap\mathcal{C}(0,T;H^2(\M)) $$ of the wave equation \begin{equation*} (\p^2_t-\Op)u=0,\quad \textrm{in}\quad Q, \end{equation*} with the initial condition \begin{equation*} u(x,0)=\p_tu(x,0)=0,\quad \textrm{in}\quad \M, \end{equation*} of the form \begin{equation} u(x,t)=\theta(x,t)\psi_a(x,t)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}+r_h(x,t), \end{equation} the remainder $r_h(x,t)$ is such that

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.2
nodes.statement_short: Insert the WKB ansatz, kill the $h^{-2}$ and $h^{-1}$ terms with the eikonal and transport equations, and estimate the remainder with the energy estimates of Lemma 1.1.
nodes.section: 3 Geometric optics solutions for the damped wave equation

nodes.name: Set up the remainder problem
nodes.statement: Let $r(x,t;h)$ solves the following homogenous boundary value problem \begin{equation} \left\{ \begin{array}{llll} \para{\partial^2_t-\Op}r(x,t)=V_h (x,t) & \textrm{in }\,\, Q,\cr r(x,0)=\p_tr(x,0)=0,& \textrm{in }\,\,\M,\cr r(x,t)=0 & \textrm{on} \,\, \Sigma. \end{array} \right. \end{equation} where the source term $V_h$ is given by \begin{equation} V_h(x,t)=-\para{\partial_t^2-\Op}\para{(\theta\psi_a)(x,t)e^{i\varphi/h}}. \end{equation} To prove our Lemma it would be enough to show that $r$ satisfies the estimates (\ref{3.25}).
nodes.statement_short: Define $r_h$ as the solution of the homogeneous boundary value problem with source $V_h$.
nodes.section: 3 Geometric optics solutions for the damped wave equation

nodes.name: Expand the source term $V_h$
nodes.statement: By a simple computation, we have \begin{align} -V_h (x,t)&=e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}\para{\p_t^2-\Op}\para{(\theta\psi_a)( x,t)}\cr &\quad -\frac{2i}{h} e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}\psi_a(x,t)\para{\p_t\theta+\seq{d\varrho,d\theta}+\frac{\theta}{2}\Delta\varrho}( x,t)\cr &\quad -\frac{2i}{h} e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}\theta(x,t)\para{\p_t\psi_a+\seq{d\varrho,d\psi_a}+\frac{a}{2} \psi_a}(x,t)\cr &\quad-\frac{1}{h^2} \theta\psi_a(x,t) e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}\para{1-\abs{d\varrho}^2}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Compute $-V_h$ as a sum of the $O(1)$ term plus $h^{-1}$ transport terms and an $h^{-2}$ eikonal term.
nodes.section: 3 Geometric optics solutions for the damped wave equation

nodes.name: Cancel the singular terms and bound $V_0$
nodes.statement:
Taking into account (ef{3.7})-(ef{3.11}) and (ef{3.12}), the right-hand side of (ef{3.28}) becomes  egin{align} V_h (x,t)&=-e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}(\p_t^2-\Op)\para{(	heta\psi_a)(x,t)} \cr &\equiv-e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}V_0(x,t). \end{align} Since $	heta\in\mathcal{V}(Q)$ and $\psi_a\in\mathcal{W}(Q)$ we deduce that $V_0\in H^1_0(0,T;L^2(\M))$. Furthermore, there is a constant $C>0$, such that  egin{equation} 
orm{V_0}_{L^2(Q)}+
orm{\p_tV_0}_{L^2(Q)}\leq C
orm{	heta}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}.
nodes.statement_short: The eikonal and transport equations remove the $h^{-2}$ and $h^{-1}$ terms, leaving $V_h=-e^{i\varphi/h}V_0$ with $V_0$ bounded in $H^1_0(0,T;L^2)$.
nodes.section: 3 Geometric optics solutions for the damped wave equation

nodes.name: Gain one power of $h$ by integrating in time
nodes.statement:
By Lemma ef{L.1.1}, we find  egin{equation} r_h\in \mathcal{C}^2(0,T;L^2(\M))\cap\mathcal{C}^1(0,T;H^1_0(\M))\cap\mathcal{C}(0,T;H^2(\M)). \end{equation} Since the coefficients $a$ and $q$ do not depend on $t$, the function $$ r^*_h(x,t)=\int_0^tr_h(x,s)ds, $$ solves the mixed hyperbolic problem (ef{3.26}) with the right side $$ V^*_h(x,t)=\int_0^tV_h (x,s)ds=-ih\int_0^tV_0(x,s)\p_s\para{e^{i\varphi(x,s)/h}}ds. $$ Integrating by part with respect to $s$, we conclude that $$ 
orm{V^*_h}_{L^2(Q)}\leq Ch
orm{	heta}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}. $$ and by (ef{1.5}), we get  egin{eqnarray} 
orm{r_h(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\M)}=
orm{\p_tr^*_h(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\M)}\leq Ch
orm{	heta}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 1.1 to the primitive $r_h^*=\int_0^t r_h$, whose source gains a factor $h$ after integration by parts.
nodes.section: 3 Geometric optics solutions for the damped wave equation

nodes.name: Collect the remainder estimates
nodes.statement_short: Re-apply the energy estimates at orders one and two and sum (3.32)-(3.34) to obtain (3.25).
nodes.section: 3 Geometric optics solutions for the damped wave equation

nodes.name: Lemma 3.3 (backward geometric optics solutions)
nodes.statement: Let $a\in W^{2,\infty}(\M)$, $q\in W^{2,\infty}(\M)$, and $\theta\in\mathcal{V}(Q)$, $\psi_{-a}\mathcal{W}(Q)$ solve respectively (\ref{3.11}) and (\ref{3.12}) (with $a$ replaced by $-a$). Then for all $h>0$ small enough, there exists a solution $$ u(x,t;h)\in \mathcal{C}^2(0,T;L^2(\M))\cap\mathcal{C}^1(0,T;H^1(\M))\cap\mathcal{C}(0,T;H^2(\M)) $$ of the wave equation \begin{equation*} (\p^2_t-\Opp)u=0,\quad \textrm{in}\quad Q, \end{equation*} with the final condition \begin{equation*} u(T,x)=\p_tu(T,x)=0,\quad \textrm{in}\quad \M, \end{equation*} of the form \begin{equation} u(x,t;h)=\theta(x,t)\psi_{-a}(x,t)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}+r_h(x,t), \end{equation} the remainder $r_h(t,x)$ is such that \begin{align*} r_h(x,t)&=0,\quad (x,t)\in \Sigma , \\ r_h(x,T)=\p_tr_h(x,T)&=0,\quad x\in \M. \end{align*} Furthermore, there exist $C>0$, $h_0>0$ such that, for all $h \leq h_0$ the following estimates hold true. \begin{equation} \sum_{k=0}^2 \sum_{j=0}^{k} h^{k-1} \|\p_t^{j} r_h(\cdot,t)\|_{H^{k-j}(\M)}\leq C\norm{\theta}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}. \end{equation} The constant $C$ depends only on $T$ and $\M$ (that is $C$ does not depend on $a$ and $h$).
nodes.statement_short: Same construction for the backward equation with $-a$ and vanishing final data at $t=T$.

assumptions: Let $a\in W^{2,\infty}(\M)$, $q\in W^{2,\infty}(\M)$, and $\theta\in\mathcal{V}(Q)$, $\psi_{-a}\mathcal{W}(Q)$ solve respectively (\ref{3.11}) and (\ref{3.12}) (with $a$ replaced by $-a$)
conclusions: there exists a solution $$ u(x,t;h)\in \mathcal{C}^2(0,T;L^2(\M))\cap\mathcal{C}^1(0,T;H^1(\M))\cap\mathcal{C}(0,T;H^2(\M)) $$ of the wave equation \begin{equation*} (\p^2_t-\Opp)u=0,\quad \textrm{in}\quad Q, \end{equation*} with the final condition \begin{equation*} u(T,x)=\p_tu(T,x)=0,\quad \textrm{in}\quad \M, \end{equation*} of the form \begin{equation} u(x,t;h)=\theta(x,t)\psi_{-a}(x,t)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}+r_h(x,t), \end{equation} the remainder $r_h(t,x)$ is such that

nodes.name: Standing assumptions on the two pairs of coefficients
nodes.statement: As before, we let $a_1,\,a_2\in\mathscr{A}(m_1,\eta)$ and $q_1,q_2\in\mathscr{Q}(m_2)$ such that $a_1=a_2$, $q_1=q_2$ near the boundary $\p\M$. We set $$ a(x)=(a_1-a_2)(x),\quad q(x)=(q_1-q_2)(x). $$ Recall that we have extended $a_{1},a_{2}$ as $W^{2,\infty}(\M_1)$ in such a way that $a=0$ and $q=0$ on $\M_{1} \setminus \M$.\\ We denote $\psi_{a_2}\in\mathcal{W}(Q)$ and $\psi_{-a_1}\in\mathcal{W}(Q)$ the solutions of (\ref{3.12}) respectively with $a=a_2$ and $a=-a_1$ given by (\ref{3.22}), and set \begin{equation} \psi_a(x,t)=\psi_{a_2}(x,t)\psi_{-a_1}(x,t). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Set $a=a_1-a_2$, $q=q_1-q_2$ (both vanishing outside $\M$) and $\psi_a=\psi_{a_2}\psi_{-a_1}$.

nodes.statement_short: The weighted integral of $a$ against products of amplitudes is bounded by $C(h+h^{-2}\|\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}\|)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement_short: Pair a forward geometric optics solution for $(a_2,q_2)$ against a backward one for $(-a_1,q_1)$, integrate by parts to produce the D-N difference, and estimate all remainder terms.

nodes.name: Construct the forward solution $u_2$
nodes.statement:
First, if $	heta_2$ satisfies (ef{3.11}), $\psi_{a_2}$ satisfies (ef{3.12}), and $h<h_0$, Lemma ef{L.3.2} guarantees the existence of a geometrical optics solution $u_2$  egin{equation} u_2(x,t)=(	heta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}+r_{2,h}(x,t), \end{equation} to the wave equation corresponding to the coefficients $a_2$ and $q_2$, $$ \para{\p^2_t-\Ops}u(x,t)=0\quad 	extrm{in}\,Q, \quad u(\cdot,0)=\p_tu(\cdot,0)=0 \quad 	extrm{in}\,\, \M, $$ where $r_{2,h}$ satisfies  egin{gather} h^{-1}
orm{r_{2,h}(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\M)}+
orm{\p_t r_{2,h}(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\M)}+
orm{
abla r_{2,h}(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\M)}\leq C
orm{	heta_2}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}, \ 
onumber r_{2,h}(x,t)=0,\quad orall (x,t)\in\,\Sigma. \end{gather} Moreover $$ u_2\in \mathcal{C}^2(0,T;L^2(\M))\cap \mathcal{C}^1(0,T;H^1(\M)) \cap \mathcal{C}(0,T;H^2(\M)).
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.2 gives $u_2=(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})e^{i\varphi/h}+r_{2,h}$ for the coefficients $(a_2,q_2)$.

nodes.name: Introduce $v$ with the same boundary data and set $w=v-u_2$
nodes.statement: Let us denote by $f_h$ the function $$ f_h(x,t)=(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h},\quad (x,t)\in\Sigma, $$ and we consider $v$ the solution of the following non-homogenous boundary value problem \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{array}{lll} \para{\p_t^2-\Opf} v=0, & \textrm{in}\,\, Q,\cr v(x,0)=\p_tv(x,0)=0, & \textrm{in}\,\, \M,\cr v(x,t)=u_2(x,t):=f_{h}(x,t), & \textrm{on}\,\, \Sigma. \end{array} \right. \end{equation} We let $ w=v-u_2$. Therefore, $w$ solves the following homogenous boundary value problem $$ \left\{\begin{array}{lll} \para{\p_t^2-\Opf}w(x,t)=a(x)\p_tu_2(x,t)+q(x)u_2(x,t) & \textrm{in}\,\, Q,\cr w(x,0)=\p_tw(x,0)=0, & \textrm{in}\,\, \M,\cr w(x,t)=0, & \textrm{on}\,\, \Sigma. \end{array} \right. $$ Using the fact that $a(x)\p_tu_2+q(x)u_2 \in W^{1,1}(0,T;L^2(\M))$ with $u_2(\cdot,0)=\p_t u_2(\cdot,0)\equiv 0$, by Lemma \ref{L.1.1}, we deduce that $$ w\in \mathcal{C}^1(0,T;L^2(\M))\cap \mathcal{C}(0,T;H^2(\M)\cap H^1_0(\M)).
nodes.statement_short: $w=v-u_2$ solves a homogeneous problem with source $a\p_tu_2+qu_2$.

nodes.name: Construct the backward solution $u_1$
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.3 provides $u_1=(\theta_1\psi_{-a_1})e^{i\varphi/h}+r_{1,h}$ for the backward equation with $(-a_1,q_1)$.
